meta.note: Exam-style written questions. Chapter 11 has 4 MCQs (Stage 2) and 14 long-form exercises here.

questions.question: How is a voltmeter connected in the circuit to measure the potential difference between two points?
hints: A voltmeter measures potential difference between two points.
It must not draw large current from the circuit.
questions.model_answer:
A voltmeter is connected **in parallel** across the two points between which the potential difference is to be measured.

It has very high resistance so that it takes negligible current from the branch.
marking_points: Across the two points / high resistance so negligible current
common_mistakes: Connecting voltmeter in series (confusing with ammeter)

questions.question: A copper wire has diameter 0.5 mm and resistivity of 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What will be the length of this wire to make its resistance 10 Ω? How much does the resistance change if the diameter is doubled?
hints: Use R = ρL/A with A = πr² and r = diameter/2 (in metres).
Rearrange: L = RA/ρ.
If diameter doubles, area becomes 4× larger, so R becomes 1/4 for the same length.
questions.model_answer:
ρ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, d = 0.5 mm = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m, r = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m

A = πr² ≈ 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m²

L = RA/ρ = (10 × 1.96 × 10⁻⁷) / (1.6 × 10⁻⁸) ≈ **122.5 m**

If diameter is doubled, area × 4, so for same length **R_new = 10/4 = 2.5 Ω**.
marking_points: New R = 2.5 Ω when diameter doubled
common_mistakes: Saying R doubles when diameter doubles

questions.question:
The values of current I flowing in a given resistor for the corresponding values of potential difference V across the resistor are given below:

I (A): 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0
V (V): 1.6, 3.4, 6.7, 10.2, 13.2

Plot a graph between V and I and calculate the resistance of that resistor.
hints: Plot V on y-axis and I on x-axis (or as directed — slope gives R).
Resistance R = V/I from Ohm's law.
Use a pair of well-separated points or slope of best line.
questions.model_answer:
Plot **V vs I** — straight line through origin (Ohmic conductor).

R = V/I using any row, e.g. R = 13.2/4.0 = **3.3 Ω** (or 6.7/2.0 = 3.35 Ω).

Accept **R ≈ 3.2–3.4 Ω** from graph slope.
common_mistakes: Plotting I on y-axis without adjusting slope interpretation

questions.question: When a 12 V battery is connected across an unknown resistor, there is a current of 2.5 mA in the circuit. Find the value of the resistance of the resistor.
hints: Convert mA to A: 2.5 mA = 2.5 × 10⁻³ A.
Use R = V/I.
common_mistakes: Using I = V × R instead of R = V/I

questions.question: A battery of 9 V is connected in series with resistors of 0.2 Ω, 0.3 Ω, 0.4 Ω, 0.5 Ω and 12 Ω, respectively. How much current would flow through the 12 Ω resistor?
hints: In series, the same current flows through every resistor.
Add all resistances, then I = V/R_total.
questions.model_answer:
R_total = 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.4 + 0.5 + 12 = **13.4 Ω**

I = V/R_total = 9/13.4 ≈ **0.67 A**

Same current **0.67 A** flows through the 12 Ω resistor (series circuit).
common_mistakes: Calculating current only through 12 Ω using 9 V/12 Ω

questions.question: How many 176 Ω resistors (in parallel) are required to carry 5 A on a 220 V line?
hints: Find total resistance R_total = V/I.
For n equal resistors in parallel: R_total = R/n.
questions.model_answer:
R_total = V/I = 220/5 = **44 Ω**

For n resistors of 176 Ω in parallel: 44 = 176/n

n = 176/44 = **4 resistors**

questions.question: Show how you would connect three resistors, each of resistance 6 Ω, so that the combination has a resistance of (i) 9 Ω, (ii) 4 Ω.
hints: (i) 6 + 3 = 9: two 6 Ω in parallel give 3 Ω; add one 6 Ω in series.
(ii) 4 Ω: two 6 Ω in series (12 Ω) in parallel with third 6 Ω → 4 Ω.
questions.model_answer:
(i) **9 Ω:** Two 6 Ω resistors in **parallel** (3 Ω) connected in **series** with a third 6 Ω resistor → 3 + 6 = **9 Ω**.

(ii) **4 Ω:** Two 6 Ω resistors in **series** (12 Ω) connected in **parallel** with the third 6 Ω resistor:
1/R = 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/4 → **R = 4 Ω**.
marking_points: (i) Correct combination for 9 Ω with diagram/description
Uses series and parallel rules correctly
common_mistakes: All three in series or parallel only

questions.question: Several electric bulbs designed to be used on a 220 V electric supply line, are rated 10 W. How many lamps can be connected in parallel with each other across the two wires of 220 V line if the maximum allowable current is 5 A?
hints: Maximum power P_max = V × I_max.
Each lamp takes 10 W; number = P_max / 10.
questions.model_answer:
P_max = V × I = 220 × 5 = **1100 W**

Number of 10 W lamps in parallel = 1100/10 = **110 lamps**
common_mistakes: Dividing 5 A by current of one bulb without finding bulb current first

questions.question: A hot plate of an electric oven connected to a 220 V line has two resistance coils A and B, each of 24 Ω resistance, which may be used separately, in series, or in parallel. What are the currents in the three cases?
hints: Separately: I = V/R = 220/24.
Series: R = 48 Ω; Parallel: R = 12 Ω.
I = V/R_total for each case.
questions.model_answer:
V = 220 V, each coil R = 24 Ω.

**(i) One coil only:** I = 220/24 ≈ **9.17 A**

**(ii) Series (A and B):** R = 48 Ω, I = 220/48 ≈ **4.58 A**

**(iii) Parallel (A and B):** R = 12 Ω, I = 220/12 ≈ **18.33 A**

questions.question:
Compare the power used in the 2 Ω resistor in each of the following circuits:
(i) a 6 V battery in series with 1 Ω and 2 Ω resistors, and
(ii) a 4 V battery in parallel with 12 Ω and 2 Ω resistors.
hints: (i) Series: I = 6/(1+2) = 2 A; P on 2 Ω = I²R.
(ii) Parallel across 4 V: V across 2 Ω = 4 V; P = V²/R.
questions.model_answer:
(i) **Series:** R_total = 3 Ω, I = 6/3 = 2 A
P_2Ω = I²R = 4 × 2 = **8 W**

(ii) **Parallel:** 2 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel across 4 V
P_2Ω = V²/R = 16/2 = **8 W**

**Same power (8 W)** in the 2 Ω resistor in both cases.
common_mistakes: Using wrong total resistance in parallel case
Forgetting P = V²/R when V is known across resistor

questions.question: Two lamps, one rated 100 W at 220 V, and the other 60 W at 220 V, are connected in parallel to electric mains supply. What current is drawn from the line if the supply voltage is 220 V?
hints: In parallel at 220 V, each lamp takes I = P/V.
Total current is sum of branch currents.
marking_points: Uses I = P/V for each lamp
common_mistakes: Adding powers then dividing by V (actually same here: 160/220)

questions.question: Which uses more energy, a 250 W TV set in 1 hr, or a 1200 W toaster in 10 minutes?
hints: Energy E = P × t (use same units, e.g. watt-hours).
Convert 10 minutes to hours: 10/60 h.
questions.model_answer:
TV: E = 250 W × 1 h = **250 Wh**

Toaster: E = 1200 W × (10/60) h = **200 Wh**

**250 W TV for 1 hour** uses more energy.

questions.question: An electric heater of resistance 44 Ω draws 5 A from the service mains for 2 hours. Calculate the rate at which heat is developed in the heater.
hints: Rate of heat = electric power P.
P = I²R (time is extra info for energy, not rate).
questions.model_answer:
Rate of heat developed = Power P = I²R = 5² × 44 = **1100 W**

(Also P = VI if V is known. Energy in 2 h = 1100 W × 2 h = 2.2 kWh — but question asks for **rate**.)
common_mistakes: Multiplying by 2 hours for the rate

questions.question:
Explain the following.
(a) Why is the tungsten used almost exclusively for filament of electric lamps?
(b) Why are the conductors of electric heating devices, such as bread-toasters and electric irons, made of an alloy rather than a pure metal?
(c) Why is the series arrangement not used for domestic circuits?
(d) How does the resistance of a wire vary with its area of cross-section?
(e) Why are copper and aluminium wires usually employed for electricity transmission?
hints: (a) High melting point; emits light at high temperature without melting.
(b) Alloys have higher resistivity and do not oxidise easily at high temperature.
(c) Series: one failure/open circuit stops all appliances; same current; unequal V division.
(d) R ∝ 1/A — thicker wire, lower R.
(e) Low resistivity → low energy loss; good conductors.
questions.model_answer:
(a) **Tungsten** has a very **high melting point** (~3400°C) so it glows at high temperature without melting, producing light efficiently.

(b) **Alloys** have **higher resistivity** than pure metals and **resist oxidation** at red heat, producing stable heating without melting quickly.

(c) **Domestic circuits use parallel** so each appliance gets full mains voltage and works independently. In **series**, one fault breaks the whole circuit and voltage is shared unequally.

(d) Resistance is **inversely proportional to area of cross-section** (R ∝ 1/A) — thicker wire → lower resistance.

(e) **Copper and aluminium** have **low resistivity**, are ductile, and minimise **heat loss (I²R)** in transmission lines.
marking_points: (c) Series unsuitable — independent operation and equal voltage need parallel
(e) Low resistivity, less energy loss in transmission
